section_summary: This section contains 1938 narcotics-control reports for Japanese-administered Korea, Taiwan, the Kwantung Leased Territory and the South Seas Mandate, including legislative annexes and special returns on prepared opium. It then shifts to 1940 U.S. State Department correspondence concerning the use of trade and customs pressure against Japanese-linked narcotics traffic. The section closes with the opening portion of a League of Nations publication reproducing Japan’s 1938 annual reports; that document continues beyond page 109.

people.name: Sōmei To
people.role: Doctor and author of a statistical study of opium smokers in Taiwan.

people.name: Syōren Tyo
people.role: Doctor and author of research on the effects of opium alkaloids on rabbits.

people.name: W. Cameron Forbes
people.role: Correspondent addressed as Governor Forbes who proposed using trade pressure against Japan over narcotics traffic.

people.name: Stanley K. Hornbeck
people.role: Colonel and U.S. State Department official in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs.

people.name: Mrs. Stanley K. Hornbeck
people.role: Wife of Stanley K. Hornbeck and proposed guest of Forbes at Thomasville.

subfiles.title: Report by the Government-General of Tyōsen for the Calendar Year 1938 on the Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs
subfiles.about: Reports on narcotics administration, addiction, illicit traffic, opium production and drug manufacture in colonial Korea during 1938.
subfiles.summary: The report states that prefectural clinics admitted 357 addicts and claimed that only nine remained at year’s end. It records expanded poppy cultivation, large seizures of opium, prosecutions and exports to the monopoly authorities in Manchukuo and the Kwantung Leased Territory. Manufacture and distribution were placed under close government supervision, while opium smoking was reported chiefly among Chinese residents.

subfiles.title: Report by the Government-General of Taiwan for the Calendar Year 1938 on the Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs
subfiles.about: Describes Taiwan’s treatment of addicts, suppression of illicit opium and morphine traffic, coca cultivation and licensed narcotics manufacture.
subfiles.summary: The report discusses addicts returning from China, compulsory treatment at the Taihoku House of Correction and the decline of junk-borne smuggling after the Sino-Japanese conflict disrupted traffic. It supplies prosecution, occupation, confiscation and illicit-price statistics and recounts a case involving diacetylmorphine smuggled from Kobe. It also describes licensed coca cultivation and cocaine manufacture at the Sin-ei factory in Tainan Province.

subfiles.title: Report by the Kwantung Bureau for the Calendar Year 1938 on the Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs
subfiles.about: Reports on the new government monopoly for prepared opium, addiction, smuggling and narcotics control in the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: The report explains the 1938 ordinances that transferred prepared-opium manufacture to the government, rationed licensed smokers and strengthened enforcement by police, customs and monopoly officials. It records 1,454 treated drug addicts and attributes increased smuggling to refugees and travelers arriving from China and Manchukuo. The territory permitted only morphine hydrochloride manufacture, at the Dairen Drug Manufacturing Company.

subfiles.title: Annex A: Imperial Ordinance No. 84 Amending the Kwantung Opium Ordinance
subfiles.about: Amends the Kwantung Opium Ordinance to establish government manufacture and supply of prepared and medical opium and revise offenses and penalties.
subfiles.summary: Annex A, Imperial Ordinance No. 84 amending the Kwantung Opium Ordinance: government monopoly on opium, regulation of retailers and smokers, delegated powers, penalties, and extracts of the earlier ordinance.

subfiles.title: Annex B: Kwantung Bureau Order No. 8—Regulations for the Enforcement of the Kwantung Opium Ordinance
subfiles.about: Sets out detailed licensing, rationing, retailing, recordkeeping and enforcement rules for opium in the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: The order establishes permits and medical examinations for Manchurian and Chinese opium addicts, fixes daily rations and assigns each licensed smoker to a designated retailer. It regulates government supply, medical use, retailer accounts, monthly reports, disposal of remaining stocks and penalties for violations. Transitional provisions and the prescribed form of an opium-smoking permit are included.

subfiles.title: Annex C: Kwantung Bureau Order No. 69
subfiles.about: Amends the enforcement regulations by removing used prepared-opium receptacles from the disposal provision.
subfiles.summary: Annex C, Kwantung Bureau Order No. 69: deletes wording on used prepared-opium receptacles from Article 7, with the prior wording reproduced.

subfiles.title: Report by the South Seas Bureau for the Calendar Year 1938 on the Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs
subfiles.about: Reports the absence of opium addiction, illicit traffic and narcotics production in the Japanese South Seas Mandate.
subfiles.summary: The bureau states that island inhabitants were free from opium smoking and that other nationalities were strictly prohibited from the practice. It reports no addicts, illicit traffic, cultivation, drug manufacture, prepared-opium use or related offenses.

subfiles.title: Special Annual Report Concerning Prepared Opium for 1938: Taiwan
subfiles.about: Provides administrative, financial and statistical information on Taiwan’s licensed prepared-opium system during 1938.
subfiles.summary: Taiwan reported compulsory treatment and police surveillance, 10,884 licensed smokers and reduced smuggling following disruption of traffic with China. The report covers research, after-care, dross disposal, confiscations, morphine substitution and revised government prices. Financial tables and production, consumption, stock, nationality, retail-shop and prosecution figures are also supplied.

subfiles.title: Special Annual Report Concerning Prepared Opium for 1938: Kwantung Leased Territory
subfiles.about: Provides administrative, medical, financial and statistical information on prepared opium in the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: The report describes strict licensing, government manufacture and cooperation among police, customs and monopoly officials, with 21,373 licensed smokers remaining at the end of 1938. It details treatment at the Kwantung Clinic, the occupations and treatment outcomes of patients, seizures and the growing substitution of morphine for opium. Tables give government revenue, expenditures, production of Hukujukō, raw-opium sources, consumption, shops and convictions.

subfiles.title: Department of State Note Transmitting Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 4313 and Japan’s 1938 Narcotics Report
subfiles.about: Transmits a copy of a Tokyo Embassy despatch and Japan’s annual report on opium and dangerous drugs for 1938.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury Tokyo despatch no. 4313 (December 11, 1939) enclosing Japan's 1938 annual narcotics report.

subfiles.title: Letter from W. Cameron Forbes to Stanley K. Hornbeck Forwarding a Narcotics Proposal
subfiles.about: Forwards Forbes’s enclosed proposal about using the narcotics issue in U.S. policy toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Forbes asks Hornbeck whether his enclosed narcotics letter merits the Secretary's attention, and invites the Hornbecks to Thomasville.

subfiles.title: Enclosed Letter from W. Cameron Forbes to the Secretary of State on Trade Pressure and Japanese Narcotics
subfiles.about: Proposes restricting Japanese trade and subjecting Japanese ships to delays and searches until Japanese-controlled narcotics production is curtailed.
subfiles.summary: Forbes argues Japanese narcotics threaten other countries, proposing extra trade impediments, extensive ship searches and publicity on drug encouragement among Chinese.

subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to W. Cameron Forbes on Narcotics Enforcement and U.S.–Japan Relations
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Forbes’s proposal and explains existing American enforcement measures against drug smuggling connected with Japanese shipping and territories.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck replies that narcotics were considered in abrogating the Japanese treaty, Japanese ships get special scrutiny, and Japanese-controlled China is a more important drug source than Japan proper.

subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to W. Cameron Forbes Acknowledging the Secretary’s Consideration
subfiles.about: Notifies Forbes that his February 6 letter was brought to the Secretary of State’s attention.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck conveys the Secretary’s thanks for Forbes’s interest and suggestions. The short letter closes with the Secretary’s best wishes.

subfiles.title: League of Nations: Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs—Annual Reports by Governments for 1938, Japan
subfiles.doc_type: League of Nations circular and report
subfiles.to: Parties to the 1931 Convention, other states and the Advisory Committee on Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs
subfiles.about: Communicates Japan’s 1938 reports on opium and dangerous drugs to governments and the League’s narcotics advisory body.
subfiles.summary: The publication begins with Japan proper, covering addicts, international trade controls, cooperation with the United States and Great Britain, offenses, confiscations, cultivation and licensed manufacture. It then reproduces the Tyōsen report and begins the Taiwan report, including addiction treatment, illicit traffic, coca cultivation and manufacturing controls. The Taiwan portion continues beyond page 109.
